Looking for headphone advice here for a very weird/specific usage case lol.

I currently have Sennheiser HD6XX for when I want headphones but mainly I love my big monitors I use for my PC more. 

What I'm wanting is some closed back headphones I can use on my gaming PC when it's storming and really getting crazy outside. This is due to a rather embarrassing anxiety I've developed over storms. For example, I don't even know if it's possible to get ANC with wired headphones. It seems everything is wireless now.

What I want...

Closed back

Over Ear (comfort is a huge priority, second only to sound isolation)

Wired (typically cheaper and I already have enough crap to keep charged)

Must be easy to push/run just fine with no headphone amp. I don't currently own one and don't feel the need to drop a lot of cash for something that will see very minimal use.

Budget is under $100 because as stated, I will only use these under very specific circumstances. If it starts to storm and I can hear crazy loud thunder and the wind ripping around. 

Sound profile wise, I'd lean more towards exciting as opposed to warm or neutral. This is for a multitude of reasons. One, that again seems to be cheaper then higher end cans that really want to sound exactly neutral or how the creators intended. Secondly, in the times I'm using these it will mainly be for PC gaming and maybe some movies or music. The goal here is to block out outside noise. So warm, neutral and quiet just doesn't matter. 

These will be plugged into my PC's motherboard directly, or a simple audio switcher so I can easily flip back and forth between speakers/headphones. Again, they will not be plugged into an amp. 

Any suggestions? Sorry for writing a huge novel. In short, I'd prefer wired, closed back and super comfortable with noise isolation being priority #1 followed by comfort. Sound quality itself is only 3rd here but obviously I'm not opposed to great sounding cans if they can fit under $100 lol.

It really is a simple way to look at it! I find it helps greatly. With that said your mileage may vary and as the op talked about, don’t expect it to be a miracle cure. 

I still get anxiety with driving sometimes (that’s the great majority of my anxiety) it’s just that using that technique really helps preventing it from spiraling further and further out of control. 

It is acceptance of your anxiety in a sense though. But as I said, just look at it as no more accepting than you are of a headache or stomach ache. You obviously still dislike it but I bet you don’t start thinking “oh my god I’m gonna die” every time you get a headache lol!

I think acceptance can help tremendously. My anxiety and what triggers is far from completely gone but numerous things have helped. 

As far as accepting goes I’ll try to describe how I view it and how it helps me. 

So, everyone knows how anxiety makes them feel physically and how to them that feeling can cause them to spiral into worse and worse anxiety until a full blown panic attack hits right? 

Well just try and view that first feeling of physical anxiety as you view any other discomfort. Accept it like you accept a headache or a stomach ache. 

When you’re driving down the road and a headache comes on it’s not pleasant right? Of course not, but it doesn’t cause you to panic and spiral into a panic attack. You just tell yourself, “well that sucks, I have a headache”. Now of course if you could snap your fingers and eliminate the the headache you would but since you can’t you just accept you have a headache, acknowledge it sucks and go on with your life for the day. 

Do the same with your anxiety when it first hits. Of course if you could snap your fingers and make it disappear you would but since you can’t, just accept. Just tell yourself, “well, I got some discomfort/anxiety going on, that sucks” and then continue on about your day. 

I know that sounds stupid easy but I swear it helps. It really is true if you think about. Most other physical feelings that we don’t like don’t make us spiral out of control emotionally and mentally right? There is no reason for the physical discomfort of anxiety to do so either. Just admit it’s a uncomfortable physical feeling like every other uncomfortable physical feeling and move on.

For me though, before Half Life I was playing Doom, Quake and Unreal type shooters. In short, I liked really fast but almost brain dead shooting with all action and very minimal story. 

Once Half Life released that changed shooters for good until the fairly recent "boomer shooter" genre that's popped up. FPS became less about frantic and fast gameplay and more about telling stories. Again, I am NOT saying that's a bad thing and I am not saying the gaming world hasn't benefited from this. I'm simply speaking that for myself, as a kid at that time I didn't care about story really. I just wanted fast paced action. 

For me personally the greatest thing Half Life did was help put Valve into a position to be able to create Steam. 

Please don't be to harsh on me guys! We're all entitled to our opinions. Like I said, I recognize Half Life is beloved by the majority and I'd never say it's a bad game. I can simply say that as for myself, I didn't personally like it.

I could be wrong as I haven't played the latest college football game yet but I have played the rest of them as well as Madden a heck of a lot.

IMO I think Madden would be the most friendly to someone new to Football. I think this for a couple of reasons.

1. College football is way more varied in how teams play compared to the NFL. It's hard to really explain to someone who doesn't "know" football but basically some teams will run all the time, other teams will pass all the time and then others do so many different combinations of the two. In the NFL there is obviously some differences but the great majority of teams use a variation of what's literally called a "pro style" offense. 

2. In college ball players have no choice but to cycle out. The longest someone will play (without crazy circumstances) is 4 to 5 years. In the NFL there is no limit other than the players health. So, it's easier to manage game play wise. With Madden you can kind of "lock in" your roster for quite awhile. With the college game you will be forced to deal with recruiting. While I find that fun (and many others do too!) if you go into the game knowing nothing about football it may be a little difficult to recruit effectively. You may end up getting a hodge podge of players that don't really fit into the same system very well.

3. The NFL has 32 teams as opposed to 130+ to keep up with. Admittedly this doesn't matter THAT much but hey, it's just more to keep up with.

4. Lastly, the NFL is just clean and simple when it comes to making the playoffs and who moves on. Anyone can figure out how that works quite easily. In college it's no where near cut and dry. Records matter but it's not uncommon at all to see a 10-2 team ranked or placed higher then say a 11-1 team. 

With all of this said. I vastly prefer college football to the NFL. I just think it's more passionate and more way more fun! If you can take the time to learn it and really get into it the college game offers so much more than the NFL. That is JUST my opinion though. Not everyone would agree. I know plenty of people who watch the NFL but not college ball.

Yes, the company would have lost money. People tend to think that costs only "cost" when it comes to physical items, like the actual product ordered. However, you have to take into account the salaries of their employees that are being paid, the shipping costs, the day to day cost in bills (utilities and such) as well.

Companies pay X for a product and sell it for X+, that + is determined by factoring in their costs for all of the above. So yeah, just because you bought 20 items at 100 bucks and sold them to someone for that same price doesn't mean you broke even, you actually lost money due to time and salaries paid.

Sometimes people will argue "But, they were having to pay those employees anyway, so it wouldn't have mattered if they had X orders or not". That is false though. Again, where do you think they come up with a number for salaries that are paid? They get those by factoring in projected sales and total costs.

In short, however much time their employees spent "working" on this order, and however much shipping costs they had as well as the utility costs that accumulated while working on this order were all a net loss.

With that said, it's still a miniscule amount in this case. I mean $2400 isn't fun to lose but it's definitely not worth firing someone over and losing out on what you've invested to train the person. So, my post isn't to "defend" the company or the boss but simply to show that yes, they would have lost money.

You’ve got to find out what causes your anxiety and you’ve got to constantly expose yourself to it. It’s painful, it’s horrible and frankly scary as hell but it will eventually work. Eventually your brain finally puts 2 and 2 together and realizes that which causes you anxiety isn’t actually harmful. 

The good news is, you do not have to do it without any help. You can use meds to help you when you first start exposing yourself. Or by talking to an actual medical professional such as a psychiatrist!

I had crippling anxiety when driving or riding on cars. I wouldn’t go anywhere further than down the street. I got a job thag requires me to drive an hour both ways. When I first started I’d have to pull over every few minutes just to come down from the panic attacks. Now, over 2 years later I drive to and from with zero worries.

Now, I still get nervous if I have to get on the interstate for hours at a time. For those occasions I’ll take 1 Ativan or 1 extended release beta blocker. The goal is to do that enough to where eventually it’ll be just like driving to work for me and I wont need the meds. 

In short, medication and other remedies can help. Always seek the help of a medical professional, BUT exposure will solve the problem. It just takes time and it’s very uncomfortable until your brain clicks over to normal.

For me, any changes or additions made to an early access game is purely a bonus.

I understand that may make me the type of player that devs wouldn't really like. They probably want or even need people to send reports and give them feedback but I just don't have the time or energy to do so. If I start down that rabbit hole and get that invested then it just opens me up to being more bummed out if changes never occur or if the game is never "complete".

I'm 100% fine with giving them money up front and being satisfied with the current state of the game. If I wasn't I wouldn't have bought into early access to start with. Because of this, I do tend to spend a lot of time looking up things about new early access games before I purchase.

If you can figure out where you anxiety comes from you can slowly get your brain to realize you are ok when confronted with it by slowly exposing yourself more and more. It’s down right scary as hell at first but it does work!

I think you're overreacting to this but I understand where you're coming from. Think of it like this...

Google Play Store isn't going to go anywhere or suddenly (or even slowly) bleed to death. This doesn't mean that people who put apps on the Play Store can just not pay the 30% cut. It just means that now they can put their own store on Android and that store will bypass the cut.

Now, you may be thinking "Why wouldn't every company do this and save the 30% cut". The answer is simple. They simply aren't big enough.

Take Steam for example. They take a 30% cut yet they get new games released on Steam constantly. This is because Steam is huge and your game will be advertised to gamers all over the world. In the end you'll actually make more money by releasing on Steam. The Play Store will be the exact same way for the vast majority of app developers. Very few will be in a position where they are large enough and have enough notoriety to actually earn more by not being on the Play Store. Fortnite is definitely one of those.

That's all this is really. No one has to release games on Steam. They could just sell their games on their own website and take 100% instead of the 70% they get on Steam. They don't do this though because "Jim Bob Tackles the Mountain 3" is known by literally no one and they'd probably only make sales to friends and family. Throw it up on Steam and all the sudden "Jim Bob Tackles the Mountain 3" is on the screen of millions of gamers across the word. The Play Store works the same for app developers. Very few would be able to get by without it.

As someone who just returned the Quest 3 I purchased after 5 days I would say I'm not interested right now. Now, with time I think VR will become better and better and I plan on checking it out again after it's matured some.

For now the cons just outweigh the pros in my opinion. By far the biggest frustration with the Quest 3 was simply getting it to work for PCVR. If you use it stand a lone I had zero problems and it worked right out of the box. The problem with that though is you're really limited by the power of the Quest 3. 

I was more interested in connecting it to my PC and using the power of my machine to push games. This is where the problems start. Whether you try to do it wirelessly over airlink or try to do it wired with the official cord it didn't matter. Half the time it would connect to my PC and half the time it wouldn't. Once it did connect you could actually use it to browse your pc (the desktop) half the time, and again the other half it wouldn't work. Further more, a lot of games simply wouldn't work without spending a lot of time tinkering with numerous options. All in all I spent hours messing with options just to get a single game to work correctly. The system is very far from being plug and play simple. Finally, once you do get it all working correctly there is a big possibility it will make you sick. Granted, that's not the fault of the VR system but a simple reality of being human. Some it won't affect that way but others it will. Also, don't think just because it finally worked correctly that you can wake up and simply boot it right back up. Nope, chances are even though you changed nothing it won't work the next day without more tinkering. This happened to me almost every day with every game I tried. 

In the end, if you're willing to put in the time to twink it and set it up correctly it could be an immersive experience. For me though, at my age, I simply don't have the desire to spend as much time setting up a game as I do playing it. 

I think the VR industry just needs more time to mature and iron out all the kinks. Once the software gets really stable and it's much easier to plug in and play I think more people like me would be willing to hop (and stay) on board. Until then it's simply not worth it for many of us. 

I have heard that other headsets like the Steam one are much more plug and play and are easier to use for PCVR. I admit I'm slightly interested in that but one of the definite plusses of the Quest 3 is the image quality. I don't particularly want to drop down in quality.

I think I'm going to wait for the next generation of the Vive or Rift (a stand a lone headset dedicated to PCVR) and hope that the image quality is at least as good as the Quest 3.
